steps.text: Part 4 of 5: What did their last move threaten?. This part covers Make it, stop it, see it. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

You make threats too, and every threat costs your opponent a move. The best ones are quiet: they improve your position *and* ask a question your opponent must answer. [H] At our level people often make a threat by accident, then forget to follow it up. Saying 'my move threatens...' aloud may fix that. I have not tested this.
steps.chapter: Make it, stop it, see it

steps.caption: White to move. Nothing is attacked on either side. Make a threat with a developing move.

line.say: The rook takes the open file and now attacks the loose pawn on d5.
Black spends a move on its king, so the threat has already cost Black time.

claims.statement: At the start, Black threatens nothing.
After the rook move the pawn on d5 is attacked and unguarded.

steps.caption: The position after the rook move. Black to move. What if Black ignores it?

line.say: The rook takes the pawn that nothing guarded.

claims.statement: If Black passes, the rook wins the pawn.

steps.text: The same question protects you from your own moves: *what would they threaten after I play this?* Dan Heisman, as reported in a chess.com article [S], uses 'hope chess' for moving and hoping the reply is harmless, and suggests looking at forcing replies first. A move can leave a piece loose that it used to guard.

steps.caption: White to move. The rook attacks the bishop, and the knight is its only guard. A developing move tempts.

line.say: The knight develops, and that takes away the bishop's only guard.
The rook takes the bishop and nothing takes back.

claims.statement: Now no white piece is loose: the knight guards the bishop.
After the knight leaves, the bishop is loose.
The developing move is a clear mistake.

steps.caption: Same position. Ask the question first, then pick a move that keeps the knight where it is. Kf1, b3 and a3 all do.

line.say: The king steps towards the centre, and the knight keeps guarding the bishop.
Black has found nothing to take.

claims.statement: After the king move, no white piece is loose.
After b3 no white piece is loose either.
The knight still guards the bishop.
